entities.name: Congress
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Argentine National Congress (Congreso de la Nación Argentina), the bicameral legislature comprising the Chamber of Deputies (257 members elected for 4-year terms, half renewed every 2 years) and the Senate (72 senators, 3 per province and Buenos Aires City, 6-year terms), established by the 1853 Constitution of Argentina, is the legislative institution of Latin America's third-largest economy and one of the region's most politically volatile democracies — having experienced 6 complete democratic breakdowns through military coups in the 20th century.

Argentina's Congress has operated under interrupted democratic conditions: military coups in 1930, 1943, 1955, 1962, 1966, and 1976 suspended congressional activity at various intervals, most devastatingly under the 1976-1983 military dictatorship that disappeared approximately 30,000 people. The restoration of democracy in 1983 under Raúl Alfonsín was followed by constitutional reform in 1994 (under President Carlos Menem's Pacto de Olivos) which introduced direct presidential election, PASO primary elections, and a third Senator per province.

Argentina's Congress has been the arena for some of Latin America's most dramatic political crises: the 2001-2002 economic collapse and default (when Congress selected three presidents in two weeks during December 2001 street protests), and the Peronist-vs.-non-Peronist political polarization that has defined Argentine politics since 1946. The Kirchnerismo era (Néstor Kirchner 2003-2007, Cristina Fernández de Kirchner 2007-2015) used congressional majorities to pass major economic and human rights legislation; the opposition Macri and current Milei governments reflect the pendulum of Argentine politics.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Argentina's National Congress — repeatedly suspended by six military coups, managing the 2001 economic collapse crisis through unprecedented presidential succession, and arena of Latin America's most dynamic Peronist/anti-Peronist political competition — is the central institution in one of Latin America's most turbulent yet enduring democratic traditions.
